problems.statement: The rise in admitted-patient ED length of stay is a boarding problem driven by late medical-ward discharges (bed availability) after the March 2026 hospitalist rounding change (09:30 start, new admissions first).
ED nurse understaffing is the cause of the longer length of stay (the client's presented explanation).
Overall inpatient capacity or demand shift (more visits, higher acuity, higher admission rate, fewer beds, longer inpatient stay) explains the boarding.

Discontinuing the advanced-practice provider-in-triage shift on 1 May 2026 contributes to the worse door-to-provider and left-without-being-seen rates; this is a separate, smaller front-end problem that boarding-related room shortage may also drive.
The September cut in evening bed-cleaning attendants (6 to 4) worsens bed turnaround and boarding, but it came after boarding had already plateaued and no turnaround data exist.
ED nurse workload, morale and intent to leave have worsened as a consequence of boarding (nurses providing inpatient care in ED rooms), with some lost-staff risk.

Proposed fixes work against the cause: funding travel nurses by deferring case-manager hiring, and pausing the 4 West huddle to float its charge nurse to the ED, would remove or weaken the one intervention that reduces boarding.

A misfit between the hospitalist group's needs (reduced early workload, teaching, retention) and hospital flow needs, with no cross-unit ownership of ED-to-inpatient flow, allowed a local rounding change to damage a hospital-wide output.

causalClaims.from: Hospitalist rounding change (09:30 start, new admissions first) from 2 March 2026
causalClaims.to: Later medical-ward discharge orders and departures
Longer ED boarding of admitted patients
Higher median arrival-to-departure for admitted patients (headline measure)
Higher admitted-patient ED length of stay

causalClaims.from: ED boarding (rooms occupied by admitted patients)
causalClaims.to: Fewer rooms for new patients, higher door-to-provider and left-without-being-seen
Lower ED nurse workload satisfaction and higher intent to leave
Earlier discharges and shorter boarding for 4 West beds

causalClaims.from: Lost ED nurses in spring / vacancy

actions.action: Keep the 4 West early-discharge huddle running and extend it to the other medical wards: train all hospitalists in the protocol, have case managers prepare the discharge candidate list the afternoon before, and see likely discharges first.
actions.rationale: The pilot's huddle days were set by a rotation fixed before the pilot, the day mix was comparable, and the effect was large (before-noon departures 38% vs 11%, boarding 2.3 h vs 4.6 h), and it keeps the 08:00 teaching meeting.

actions.action: Ask the hospitalist leadership and CMO to reorder rounding (likely discharges first, with discharge orders before noon) while keeping the 09:30 start and teaching block, instead of reverting to 07:00.
actions.rationale: This targets the verified mechanism and respects the hospitalists' retention concern (E7) that blocks a straight reversal.

actions.action: Assign a single executive owner for ED-to-inpatient flow and report boarding hours and medical-ward discharge-before-noon on the board scorecard alongside ED length of stay.
actions.rationale: The harm arose because a local scheduling change was not tracked against a hospital-wide measure; shared ownership closes that gap.

actions.action: Do not pause the 4 West huddle to float its charge nurse to the ED.
actions.rationale: It would remove the one tested intervention for the cause to add a small nursing offset that does not address boarding.

actions.action: Do not fund the $1.46M travel-nurse contract by deferring medical-ward case-manager hiring or reassigning the 4 West case manager.
actions.rationale: Case managers drive the discharge-list preparation and coverage is already below target, so this trades the fix for the symptom.

actions.action: Approve eight travel nurses this quarter as the main fix for the length-of-stay rise.
actions.rationale: Staffing is at grid and unchanged per visit, and about 3.0 h of the 3.2 h rise is boarding, so extra ED nurses would not reduce it.

actions.action: Consider a small, time-limited ED staffing or boarding-care support for 14:00-20:00 as relief while discharge timing is fixed, with a defined end date.
actions.rationale: Nurses are delivering inpatient care to boarders and survey signals show retention risk, but this treats the consequence, not the cause.

actions.action: Restore hours of the advanced-practice provider-in-triage shift, or test it, after hourly front-end data are produced.
actions.rationale: It may explain part of the left-without-being-seen rise, but only quarterly front-end data exist and boarding may account for much of it.

actions.action: Restore the evening bed-cleaning attendants and rebuild bed-turnaround reporting.
actions.rationale: Turnaround data after June are unavailable, so any effect is unknown, but fixing the report is cheap and low-risk.
It risks further hospitalist attrition (E7), and a discharge-first protocol may achieve the same effect.

nextEvidence: Hourly boarding, ED room occupancy and left-without-being-seen series by month (Jan-Oct 2026) to separate the effect of boarding from the loss of triage providers, plus adjusted pilot results across all wards and hospitalists
Restored bed-turnaround (clean-to-ready) times for evening hours since the July migration, compared before and after the 1 September cleaner reduction
Huddle adherence and discharge-order timing by hospitalist and ward over the next 4-6 weeks, including non-pilot wards and any effect on readmissions or hospitalist workload
output.summary: The ED length-of-stay rise is chiefly a boarding problem: about 3.0 of the 3.2 hours sit between admit decision and departure, while ED work-up time, volume, acuity, admission rate, staffing hours and inpatient stay are flat. Boarding began in March, when hospitalists moved medical-ward rounding to 09:30 and saw new admissions first, so discharges slid to the afternoon. Surgical wards did not change. A quasi-randomized pilot supports causation. Nursing strain is real but is a consequence. Travel nurses, pausing the huddle and deferring case managers would treat the symptom and weaken the fix. Expand discharge-first rounding and the huddle. Triage-provider and cleaning cuts need data.
